(Surah al-Mulk)
Thirty verses, Meccan

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion, and He is over all things Powerful.﴾ (Surah al-Mulk). It is also called al-Munjiyah (the Deliverer), because it delivers its reciter from the punishment of the grave. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he used to call it al-Mujadilah (the Disputer), because it argues on behalf of its reciter in the grave. It has thirty verses and is Meccan.

﷽

﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion, and He is over all things Powerful.﴾

As for His saying ﴿Blessed (tabaraka)﴾, we have explained it at the beginning of Surat al-Furqan. As for His saying ﴿in whose hand is the dominion (bi-yadihi al-mulk)﴾, know that this expression is used only to emphasize that He, exalted is He, is King and Owner, as one says: "The command, the prohibition, the loosening and the binding are in the hand of so-and-so," and there is no place for a physical limb in this. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "In His hand is the dominion over every existent, and He is Powerful over everything possible that has not yet come into existence." As for His saying ﴿and He is over all things Powerful﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: This verse was used as evidence by those who claim that the non-existent is a thing. They said: His saying ﴿He is over all things Powerful﴾ entails that what is within His power is a thing. That thing which is within the power of Allah, exalted is He, is either existent or non-existent. It cannot be existent, because if He were powerful over the existent, then either He would be powerful over bringing it into existence, which is impossible, since bringing into existence what already exists is impossible; or He would be powerful over annihilating it, which is also impossible, because annihilation cannot be brought about by an agent. That is because power is an effective attribute, so it must have an effect, and non-existence is pure negation, so it is impossible to make non-existence the effect of power; therefore it is impossible for annihilation to be brought about by an agent. It is established, then, that the thing which is within the power of Allah is not existent; so it must be non-existent, and it follows that this non-existent is a thing. Our companions who deny that the non-existent is a thing argued against this with the same verse. They said: There is no doubt that substance, insofar as it is substance, is a thing, and blackness, insofar as it is blackness, is a thing, and Allah is powerful over every thing. By the implication of this verse, He must be powerful over substance insofar as it is substance, and over blackness insofar as it is blackness. And when that is so, the substance being substance and the blackness being blackness is brought about by an agent, and a choosing agent must be prior to its act. Thus the existence of Allah and His essence is prior to the substance being substance or the blackness being blackness. It follows that the non-existent is not a thing, which is what was to be proven. Then the proponents of the first view answered the objection of the opponent: We do not concede that annihilation cannot be brought about by an agent; and even if we concede that, why may it not be said that the object of power which is non-existent is called a thing because it will become a thing? Although this is figurative, it is necessary to resort to it, because of the other proofs establishing that the non-existent is not a thing.

The second issue: Al-Qadi Abu Bakr, in one of his two opinions, held that the annihilation of bodies is brought about by an agent. This is the view chosen by Abu al-Hasan al-Khayyat of the Mu'tazilah and by Mahmud al-Kharazmi. The majority among us and among the Mu'tazilah held that annihilation cannot be brought about by an agent. Al-Qadi argued: Existents are things, and Allah is powerful over every thing; so He is powerful over existents. Then either He is powerful over bringing them into existence, which is impossible, since bringing into existence what already exists is impossible; or He is powerful over annihilating them, and that entails the possibility of annihilation being brought about by an agent.

The third issue: Al-Kaʿbi held that He, exalted is He, is not powerful over the like of the servant's power, and Abu ʿAli and Abu Hashim held that He, exalted is He, is not powerful over the servant's object of power. Our companions said: He, exalted is He, is powerful over the like of the servant's object of power and over other than it. They argued for this by saying: the very object of the servant's power and its like are things, and Allah is powerful over every thing; thus the correctness of one object of power existing between two powerful agents is established by this.

The fourth issue: Our companions held that there is no influence except the power of Allah, exalted is He. They refuted the view of attributing effects to natures, as the philosophers say; they refuted the view of generated effects, as the Mu'tazilah say; and they refuted the view that the servant creates his own acts. They argued for all of this by saying: the verse indicates that He, exalted is He, is powerful over every thing. So if any of the possible things occurred not by the power of Allah but by something else, that other thing would have prevented the power of Allah from having influence over what was within its capacity, and that is impossible, because whatever is other than Allah is possible and originated, and so it is weaker in power than the power of Allah, and the weaker cannot repel the stronger.

The fifth issue: This verse indicates that the God, exalted is He, is one. For if we suppose a second god, either he is able to bring something into existence or he is not able. If he is not able at all to bring anything into existence, he is not a god. And if he is able, then the object of power of that second god is a thing, and it follows that it is within the power of the first god, by His saying ﴿He is over all things Powerful﴾. Then it follows that a created thing occurs between two creators, which is impossible, because if each of them is independently capable of bringing things into existence, it follows that each would be independent of each of them, and therefore each would be in need of both of them and independent of both, and that is impossible.

The sixth issue: Jahm argued by this verse that He, exalted is He, is not a thing. He said: If He were a thing, He would be powerful over Himself, by His saying ﴿He is over all things Powerful﴾; but His being powerful over Himself is impossible; therefore His being a thing is impossible. Our companions said: Since His saying ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest as a witness?" Say: "Allah is witness"﴾ (al-Anʿam: 19) indicates that He, exalted is He, is a thing, it is necessary to specify this generality. So this verse indicates that the specified general is present in the Book of Allah, exalted is He, and it indicates that the specification of the general by rational proof is permissible, indeed actual.

The seventh issue: The majority of the Mu'tazilah held that Allah, exalted is He, is powerful over creating lying, ignorance, futility and injustice, while al-Nazzam held that He is not powerful over them. The majority argued that ignorance and lying are things, ﴿and Allah is over all things Powerful﴾, so it is necessary that He, exalted is He, be powerful over them.

The eighth issue: The people of tawhid argued that He, exalted is He, is exempt from place and direction. For if He, exalted is He, were located in one place rather than another, then that place in which He is judged to be located would be distinguished from the place in which He is judged not to be located; for if neither of the two places were distinguished from the other, it would be impossible to judge that He is located in one and not in the other. Then the distinction of one of the two places from the other in itself requires that place to be an existent matter, because pure non-existence cannot be pointed to by the senses, nor can part of it be distinguished from part of it in the senses, nor can it be the destination of the mover. Therefore, if Allah, exalted is He, were located in a place, that place would be existent; and if that place were existent, it would be a thing and would be within the power of Allah, by His saying exalted is He: ﴿and He is over all things Powerful﴾. And since the realization of that place is by the power and origination of Allah, it follows that Allah is prior in existence to the realization of that place; and when that is so, the existence of Allah from eternity is realized without any place, and He has no direction at all; and the eternal does not cease at all. It is established, then, that He, exalted is He, is exempt from place and location, from eternity and to eternity.

The ninth issue: He, exalted is He, said first: ﴿in whose hand is the dominion﴾, then after it: ﴿and He is over all things Powerful﴾. This indicates that the dominion is in His hand only if it is established that He is powerful over all things. This is what our companions say: that if the will of the servant were to take effect while the will of Allah did not, that would indicate incapacity and weakness, and that He would not be the absolute possessor of dominion. So this shows that since He is the possessor of dominion, He must be powerful over all things.

The tenth issue: al-Qadir is an intensive form of al-Qadir (the Powerful). Since He is powerful over all things, nothing whatsoever must prevent Him from bringing into existence any of His objects of power. This entails that no obligation is owed to anyone by Him; for otherwise that obligation would prevent Him from abstaining. And nothing ugly can be attributed to Him; for otherwise that ugliness would prevent Him from acting, and He would not be complete in power, and so He would not be Powerful. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 67, verse 2**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He who created death and life﴾. On this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** They said: Life is the attribute by which the one characterized by it is such that he can know and have power. They differed about death. Some people said that it is an expression for the absence of this attribute. Our companions (the Ash'aris) said that it is an existential attribute opposed to life. They argued for their view by saying that He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿He who created death﴾, and non-existence cannot be created. This is the correct position. Al-Kalbi related with his chain of narration from Ibn Abbas that God, may He be exalted, created death in the form of a white-speckled ram that does not pass by anything, and nothing smells its scent without dying. And He created life in the form of a horseman who meets it above a donkey and below a mule; it does not pass by anything, and nothing smells its scent without coming to life. Know that this must be understood as a figurative and illustrative description; otherwise, the correct position is the one we have mentioned.

**The second issue:** The reason death is mentioned before life, although life precedes death, is for several reasons:

First: Muqatil said: By death is meant a drop of semen, a clinging clot, and a lump of flesh, and by life is meant the breathing in of the spirit.

Second: Ata related from Ibn Abbas, who said: He means death in this world and life in the Hereafter, the abode of living.

Third: It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that: "A caller will call on the Day of Resurrection: 'O people of Paradise!' They will know that it is from God, the Mighty and Majestic, and they will say: 'Here we are, our Lord, at Your service!' He will say: 'Have you found what your Lord promised to be true?' They will say: 'Yes.' Then death will be brought in the form of a white-speckled ram and slaughtered. Then it will be proclaimed: 'O people of Paradise, eternal life without death! O people of the Fire, eternal life without death!' So the people of Paradise will increase in joy upon joy, and the people of the Fire will increase in grief upon grief."

Know that we have explained that death is an accident among the accidents, like stillness and motion, so it is not possible for it to become a ram; rather, what is meant is an illustration, so that it is known that on that day the matter of death has ended. From what we have mentioned it becomes clear that the days of death are the days of this world, and these are coming to an end, while the days of the Hereafter are the days of life, and these come later. Since the days of death precede the days of life, God necessarily mentioned death before life.

Fourth: He placed death before life because the person who sets his death before his eyes is the one most driven to act. Thus it was given precedence, since in what relates to the purpose it is more important.

**The third issue:** Know that life is the foundation of all blessings; were it not for it, no one would enjoy this world. It is also the foundation of the blessings of the Hereafter; were it not for it, lasting reward would not be established. Death is also a blessing, as we have explained its state in several places in this book. How could it not be, since it is the separator between the state of obligation and the state of recompense? It is a blessing from this aspect. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Increase your remembrance of the destroyer of pleasures." He also said to a people: "If you were to increase your remembrance of the destroyer of pleasures, it would occupy you from what I see." And the Prophet (ﷺ) asked about a man whom people praised, saying: "How is his remembrance of death?" They said: "Little." He said: "Then he is not as you say."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That He may test you as to which of you is best in deed, and He is the Mighty, the Forgiving﴾. On this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Ibtila' (testing) is trial and examination, so that He may know whether one obeys or disobeys. For one who must know all knowables eternally and everlastingly, such testing is impossible; however, we have examined this matter in our interpretation of His saying: ﴿And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with words﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 124). The summary is that testing from God means that He deals with His servant in a manner resembling testing, as with one being examined.

**The second issue:** Those who hold that God does an act for a purpose argued from His saying: "That He may test you." They said: This lam is the lam of purpose. A parallel is His saying: ﴿Except that they worship Me﴾ (Adh-Dhariyat: 56). Its answer: the act in itself is not a test, but since it resembles a test it is called a test figuratively. Likewise here: it resembles a purpose even though it is not in itself a purpose, so the particle of purpose is mentioned with it.

**The third issue:** Know that we have explained death and life as death in the state of being a drop, a clot, and a lump of flesh, and life after that. The aspect of testing on this interpretation is that one should know that He, may He be exalted, is the one who transferred him from death to life. Just as He did that, He must be capable of transferring him from life to death, so that he will beware of the coming of death, by which the opportunity to make up what has been missed is cut off, and in which the poor and the rich, the master and the slave, are equal. If we interpret them as death in this world and life in the Resurrection, the testing in both is more complete, because fear of death in this world is present, and even greater is fear of the consequences of life in the Resurrection. The purpose of the testing is whether one restrains oneself from vices because of this fear or not.

[Page 50]

**The fourth issue:** Concerning the connection of His saying "That He may test you" with His saying ﴿which of you is best in deed﴾, there are two views.

The first, which is the view of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj: the element connected to *ayyukum* ("which of you") is implied, and the estimation is: "That He may test you, so that He may know or see which of you is best in deed."

**The fifth issue:** *Ayyu* (أيّ) is in the nominative as a subject of the beginning, and what precedes it does not govern it, because it has the sense of interrogation. For when you say, "I do not know which of you is best," the meaning is "I do not know whether Zayd is best or 'Amr." Know that whatever does not govern what follows the hamza of interrogation does not govern *ayy* either, because the meaning is the same. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿Ask them which of them will vouch for that﴾ (Al-Qalam: 40), and the discussion of this has already preceded.

**The sixth issue:** The scholars mentioned several interpretations of ﴿best in deed﴾:

First: that it is the most sincere of deeds and the most correct, because if a deed is sincere but not correct, it is not accepted, and likewise if it is correct but not sincere. Sincerity is that it be for the sake of God, and correctness is that it be in accordance with the Sunnah.

Second: Qatadah said: "I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said: 'He says: which of you is best in intellect,'" then he said: "The most complete of you in intellect is the one who fears God most, and the best of you in contemplating what God has commanded and forbidden." It is permissible to interpret the goodness of deed as the completeness of intellect, because it follows from intellect; whoever is more complete in intellect is better in deed, as stated in the hadith of Qatadah.

Third: It is related from al-Hasan: "Which of you is most ascetic in this world and most abandoning of it?" Know that when He mentioned the matter of testing, He said after it: ﴿and He is the Mighty, the Forgiving﴾, meaning: He is the Mighty, the Overpowering, whom none who does evil deeds can overcome, the Forgiving toward whoever among the evildoers repents.

Know that His being Mighty and Forgiving is not complete except after His being capable of all that is capable and knowing all that is knowable. As for the necessity of complete power, it is so that He can bring the full recompense of each person to him, whether punishment or reward. As for the necessity of complete knowledge, it is so that He knows who is obedient and who is disobedient, so that no error occurs in delivering what is right to its deserver. Thus it is established that His being Mighty and Forgiving cannot be established except after the establishment of complete power and complete knowledge. For this reason God mentioned the proof of these two attributes in this context. And since knowing that He, may He be exalted, is capable precedes knowing that He is knowing, He necessarily mentioned first the indications of power, and second the indications of knowledge.

[Page 51]

As for the evidence of power, it is His saying: ﴿He who created seven heavens in layers﴾. On this verse there are several issues.

**First issue:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* (Zamakhshari's commentary) mentions three possible readings of *tibaqan* (in layers):

The first is that *tibaqan* means matching one another, one above another, from *taabaqa al-na'l* (he matched the sandal), when he stitched it layer upon layer. This is an attribute in the form of a verbal noun (*masdar*).

The second is that the implied sense is: possessing layers (*dhata tibaq*).

The third is that the implied sense is: they were made into layers (*tuwabiqat tibaqan*).

**Second issue:** The evidence that these heavens point to power is in several respects:

The first is that they remain suspended in the air of the atmosphere without a pillar or a chain.

The second is that each of them is specified with a determined measure, although it is possible for it to be larger or smaller.

The third is that each of them is specified with a particular motion, determined by a fixed degree of speed or slowness, toward a specific direction.

[Page 52]

The fourth is that they are in their very essence created (*muhdathah*). All of this indicates that they depend upon a Creator who is perfectly powerful.

As for the evidence of knowledge, it is His saying: ﴿You see in the creation of the Most Merciful no imbalance. Then return your gaze; do you see any rifts?﴾ On this verse there are several issues.

**First issue:** Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited *min tafawwutin* (with a gap, with a lack), and the rest recited *min tafawutin* (with imbalance). Al-Farra' said: "The two are of the same standing, like *tazahhur* and *tazahur*, and *ta'ahhud* and *ta'ahud*." Al-Akhfash said: "*Tafawut* is better, because they say *tafawata al-amr* (the matter became disproportionate), and they hardly say *tafawwata*." Abu 'Ubayda preferred *tafawwut*, and said: "It is said *tafawwata al-shay'* when the thing has passed away (*faata*)," and he argued with what is reported in a hadith: that a man *tafawwata* (lost out) on his father regarding his wealth.

**Second issue:** The real meaning of *tafawut* is lack of proportion, as if one part of a thing escapes (*yafutu*) another and does not suit it. From this is the saying of people: "A related element that is *mutafawit* (ill-fitting) is the opposite of one that is *mutanasib* (proportionate)." As for the words of the exegetes: al-Suddi said, "*Min tafawut*" means from the variation of a defect; the observer says, "If it were such, it would be better." Others said that *tafawut* means rifts (*futur*), by the evidence of His saying after it: ﴿Then return your gaze; do you see any rifts?﴾. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿and it has no openings﴾ (Qaf 50:6). Al-Qaffal said: "It is possible that the meaning is: you see in the creation of the Most Merciful no imbalance in the indication of the wisdom of its Maker, and that He did not create it in vain."

**Third issue:** The address in His saying ﴿You see﴾ is either to the Messenger or to every addressee. The same applies to His saying ﴿Then return your gaze; do you see any rifts?﴾ and ﴿Then return your gaze twice; the gaze will return to you humbled and weary﴾.

**Fourth issue:** His saying ﴿in layers﴾ is an attribute of the heavens. His later saying ﴿You see in the creation of the Most Merciful no imbalance﴾ is another attribute of the heavens. The sense is: He created seven heavens in layers, in which you see no imbalance. However, in place of the pronoun, He placed ﴿the creation of the Most Merciful﴾, to magnify their creation and to draw attention to the cause of their freedom from imbalance: that it is ﴿the creation of the Most Merciful﴾, and that by His dazzling power it is He who creates such a proportionate creation.

**Fifth issue:** Know that the way of inferring from this the perfection of God Most High's knowledge is that the senses show that these seven heavens are created bodies, in a manner of precision and perfection. Every agent whose act is precise and perfected must necessarily be knowing. Thus this inference indicates that He, Most High, is knowing of all knowable things. His saying ﴿You see in the creation of the Most Merciful no imbalance﴾ points to their being precise and perfected.

**Sixth issue:** Al-Ka'bi argued with this verse that sins are not part of God Most High's creation. He said: "Because He, Most High, negated imbalance in His creation, and the intended meaning is not the negation of imbalance in size, greatness, deficiency, or defect. Therefore it is necessary to interpret it as the negation of imbalance in His creation from the standpoint of wisdom. Thus it indicates, from this aspect, that the acts of servants are not part of His creation, given the imbalance in them, some of which is ignorance, some of which is lying, and some of which is folly."

The answer: Rather, we interpret it to mean that there is no *tafawut* (lack) in it in relation to Him, since all of it is possible for Him according to power, will, and motive, and nothing in Him is ever deemed ugly. So why is interpreting the verse as referring to imbalance in the aspect you mentioned preferable to interpreting it as negating imbalance in the aspect we mentioned? Furthermore, God Most High emphasized the explanation that they are precise and perfected, and said: ﴿Then return your gaze; do you see any rifts?﴾. The meaning is that when He said ﴿You see in the creation of the Most Merciful no imbalance﴾, it was as if He said afterward: "Perhaps you do not judge by this on the basis of a single glance, and do not rely on it, because error may occur in a single look. Rather, return your gaze and repeat the look once more, until you are certain that there is absolutely no imbalance in the creation of the Most Merciful."

[Page 53]

*Futur* is the plural of *fatr*, which means a split. It is said: *fatarahu fanfatar* (he split it and it split), and from this comes *fatara nab al-ba'ir* (the camel's tooth broke through), just as it is said *shaqqa*, and its meaning is that he split the flesh and it came out. The exegetes said: ﴿Do you see any rifts?﴾, that is, any openings, cracks, fissures, and tears. All of these are their words.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then return your gaze twice; your gaze will return to you humbled while it is fatigued.﴾

He was commanded to repeat the gaze over the creation of the Most Merciful, by way of scrutinizing and tracing, to see whether he would find in it any defect or flaw. That is to say: when you repeat your look, your gaze will not return to you with what you sought of finding a flaw or defect; rather it will return to you khasi'an, that is, distanced, from your saying "khasa'tu al-kalb" (I drove the dog away) when you push it far off. Al-Mubarrad said: "al-khasi'" is the one who is distanced and humiliated. Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-khasi'" is the one who has not seen what he desires. As for "al-hasir," Ibn 'Abbas said: it is "al-kalil" (the weary). Al-Layth said: "al-hasr" and "al-husur" mean exhaustion (al-i'ya'). Al-Wahidi mentioned two possibilities here:

The first: that "al-hasir" is a passive form (maf'ul) from "hasara al-'ayn" (the distance of the seen object wearied the eye), as Ru'ba said:

"Its expanse wearies the eye's glance."

The second: the saying of al-Farra': that it is an active form (fa'il) from "al-husur," which is exhaustion (al-i'ya'). The meaning is that even if he repeats the gaze and returns it again, he will not find any defect or breach; rather the gaze returns humbled from weariness and exhaustion. Here there are two questions:

The first question: How can the gaze return "khasi'an hasiran" by returning it "twice, two times"? The answer: the dual form here is for repetition in great number, like their saying "labbayka wa sa'dayk" (at Your service again and again), meaning successive responses.

The second question: What is the meaning of ﴿Then return﴾? The answer: He commanded him to return the gaze, then commanded him not to be content with the first return, but to pause after it and fix his gaze, then return it and repeat it until his gaze becomes weary from much repetition, for he will not discover any breach at all.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 67, verse 5:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have adorned the nearest heaven with lamps, and We have made them as missiles against the devils, and We have prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze.﴾

Know that this is the second proof that He, may He be exalted, is capable and knowing. The reason is that these stars, considered as created things and as specified with a particular magnitude, a fixed position and a fixed course, indicate that their Maker is capable. And considering that they are firmly made and perfected, suited to the interests of the servants in that they are an adornment for the people of this world and a means for their benefit, they indicate that their Maker is knowing. A parallel to this verse is in Surat al-Saffat: ﴿Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven with an adornment of the stars﴾ ﴿and a protection from every rebellious devil﴾ (al-Saffat: 7). Here there are several issues:

[p. 53]

The first issue: ﴿the nearest heaven﴾ means the closest, because it is the heaven nearest to people. Its meaning is "the heaven nearest to people." Al-masabih (the lamps) are the lanterns, and the stars have been named by them. People adorn their mosques and houses with lamps, so it is said: "We have adorned the ceiling of the house in which you have gathered with lamps," meaning with lamps whose brightness your lamps cannot rival. As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and We have made them as missiles against the devils﴾, know that rujum is the plural of rajm, which is a verbal noun used to name that with which something is stoned. They mentioned two views concerning this verse:

The first view: when the devils wished to eavesdrop, they were pelted with them. If it is said: making the stars an adornment of the heaven requires their remaining and continuity, while making them missiles against the devils and throwing them at them requires their disappearance, and combining the two is contradictory. We say: the meaning of pelting the devils is not that they are struck with the bodies of the stars. Rather, it is permissible that flames separate from the stars with which the devils are struck, and those flames are the meteors (shuhub), and that is nothing but a brand taken from a fire, while the fire remains.

The second view, concerning the explanation of the stars being missiles against the devils: We made them conjectures and missiles based on the unseen against the devils of mankind, namely the astrologers (al-ahkamiyyun min al-munajjimin) who make judgments from the stars.

The second issue: know that the apparent meaning of this verse does not indicate that these stars are fixed in the nearest heaven. The reason is that if the heavens are transparent, then the stars, whether they are in the nearest heaven or in other heavens above it, must appear in the nearest heaven and shine from it. So under both assumptions the nearest heaven is adorned with these lamps.

Know that the astronomers (ashab al-hay'a, i.e., those who study the structure of the heavens) agreed that these fixed stars are fixed in the eighth sphere, which is above the spheres of the planets. They argued for this by saying that some of these fixed stars are in the eighth sphere, so all of them must be there. We said that some of them are in the eighth sphere because the fixed stars that are near the zodiac are eclipsed by these planets, so the eclipsed fixed stars must be above the eclipsing planets. And we said that since these fixed stars are in the eighth sphere, all of them must be there, because all of them move with one slow motion, one degree every hundred years, so they must be fixed in one sphere.

Know that this argument is weak, for it does not follow from the fact that some fixed stars are above the planets that all of them are there. For it is not unlikely that there is a sphere beneath the moon which, in slowness, is equal to the sphere of the fixed stars, and the stars fixed in what lies around the two poles are fixed in this lower sphere; for it is not unlikely that there are two spheres differing in smallness and largeness while being similar in motion. Under this assumption, it is not impossible that these lamps are fixed in the nearest heaven. Thus it has been established that the doctrine of the philosophers (al-falasifa) in this matter is weak.

The third issue: know that the benefits of the stars are many. Among them: God, may He be exalted, adorned the heaven with them. Among them: by means of them there arises in the night a degree of light, and for this reason, when clouds thicken at night, the darkness becomes great, because the clouds veil their lights. Among them: by means of them there arises variation in the conditions of the four seasons, for they are great luminous bodies. When the sun is conjoined with a star that heats in summer, summer becomes more intense in heat, like a fire added to another fire, for there is no doubt that the effect resulting from the combination is stronger. Among them: He, may He be exalted, made them signs by which one is guided in the darkness of land and sea, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and by the star they are guided﴾ (al-Nahl: 16). Among them: He, may He be exalted, made them missiles against the devils who bring people out of the light of faith into the darknesses of disbelief. It is narrated that the reason for this is that the jinn used to eavesdrop on news of the heaven, but when Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, the heaven was guarded and the devils were watched. Whoever among them came eavesdropping was struck with a meteor and burned, lest he descend with it to the earth and convey it to the people, thereby confusing the Prophet's matter and making people doubt his report. This is the reason for the falling of meteors, and it is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and We have made them as missiles against the devils﴾. Some people have criticized this on several grounds:

The first: the falling of stars is mentioned in the books of the ancient philosophers. They said: when the earth is heated by the sun, a dry vapour rises from it, and when it reaches the fire below the sphere, it is burned by it, and that flame is the shihab (meteor).

The second: how is it possible for these jinn to witness one, or a thousand, of their kind eavesdropping and burning, and yet they return to the same deed? For the intelligent person, when he sees destruction in a thing once, or repeatedly, or a thousand times, refrains from returning to it without benefit.

The third: it is said that the thickness of the heaven is a distance of five hundred years. If these jinn penetrate the body of the heaven and break its continuity, this is false, for He has denied that there are any rifts in it, as He said: ﴿Then look again; do you see any rifts?﴾. And if they do not penetrate the body of the heaven, how can they hear the secrets of the angels from that great distance? Moreover, if it is possible for them to hear their speech from that great distance, then they would not fail to hear the speech of the angels while they are on earth.

The fourth: the angels only came to know the future states either because they perused them in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or because they received them from the revelation of God, may He be exalted, to them. Under both assumptions, why did they not remain silent about mentioning them, so that the jinn would not be able to learn of them?

The fifth: the devils are created from fire, and fire does not burn fire but strengthens it, so how can it be conceived that the devils were restrained from eavesdropping by these meteors?

The sixth: this prohibition was for the sake of prophethood, so why did it continue after the death of the Messenger, upon whom be prayers and peace?

The seventh: these missiles only occur near the earth, as evidenced by the fact that we observe their motion with the eye. Had they been near the sphere, we would not have observed their motion, just as we do not observe the motions of the stars. Since it is established that these meteors occur near the earth, how can it be said that they prevent the devils from reaching the sphere?

The eighth: if these devils were able to convey news of the angels from the unseen to the soothsayers (kahana), why do they not convey the secrets of the believers to the disbelievers, so that the disbelievers, through their knowledge of the believers' secrets, might reach harm for them?

The ninth: why did God not prevent them from ascending to the heaven from the beginning, so that there would be no need to repel them from the heaven with these meteors?

As for the answer to the first question: we do not deny that these meteors existed before the sending of the Prophet (ﷺ) for other causes. However, that does not preclude that after the sending of the Prophet, peace be upon him, they may occur for another cause, namely the repelling and restraining of the jinn. It is narrated that it was said to al-Zuhri: Were they pelted in the pre-Islamic period? He said: Yes. It was said: What then of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And we used to sit in it on certain seats for listening. But whoever listens now will find a watching flame lying in wait for him﴾ (al-Jinn: 9)? He said: Its matter was made severe and intensified when the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent.

As for the answer to the second question: when the decree comes, sight is blinded. When God decrees for a group of them burning because of their transgression and error, He provides them with the enticing motives in seeking the goal that move them to undertake the deed which leads to destruction and ruin.

Our companions argued from this verse that the Fire is now created, because His saying "and We have prepared" is a report about the past.

Know that He, exalted is He, explained at the beginning of the surah that He is capable of all possible things. Then He mentioned after it that, although He is capable of all things, He created what He created not for play and vanity, but for the sake of trial and testing. He explained that the purpose of this trial is that He be Mighty (ʿAzīz) toward those who persist in evil, and Forgiving (Ghafūr) toward those who repent. From this, His being Mighty and Forgiving cannot be established unless His being perfect in power and knowledge is established, and He demonstrated this by the evidences mentioned. At that point, His being capable of punishing the disobedient was established, so He said: ﴿And for those who disbelieve in their Lord is the punishment of Hell﴾, meaning: and for every one who disbelieves in Allah, of the

devils and others, is the punishment of Hell. The stoned devils are not specifically meant by this. Third distinct attribute: the first attribute is his saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When they are cast into it, they will hear from it a roaring (shahīq)﴾.

﴿Ulqū﴾ means they are thrown, as wood is thrown into a great fire and cast into it. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿the fuel of Hell﴾ (al-Anbiya’: 98). Regarding His saying ﴿they will hear from it a roaring﴾ there are several views:

First: Muqatil said: they will hear a roaring from Hell. Perhaps the intended meaning is to liken the sound of the flame of the fire to a roaring (shahīq). Al-Zajjaj said: the disbelievers hear from the fire a roaring, which is the most hideous of sounds, like the sound of a donkey. Al-Mubarrad said: it is, and God knows best, an exhalation like the exhalation of one who is enraged.

Second: ʿAtaʾ said: they hear from its people, those who were cast into it before them, a roaring.

Third: they hear from themselves a roaring, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For them therein is a groaning (zafīr) and a roaring (shahīq)﴾ (Hud: 106). The first view is the most sound.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿and it seethes (tafūr)﴾. Al-Layth said: everything that surges has seethed, and this is the seething of a cooking pot, of smoke, of anger, and of water from a spring. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it boils with them as a cauldron boils. Mujahid said: it seethes with them as abundant water seethes with a little grain. It is also possible that this is from the seething of anger. Al-Mubarrad said: one says, "I left so-and-so seething with anger," and this view is reinforced by the following verse.

The third attribute: His saying: ﴿it nearly bursts with rage (tamayyaz min al-ghayz)﴾. One says, "So-and-so is bursting with rage (yatamayyaz ghayẓan)" and "he is trembling with rage (yataʿaṣṣaf ghayẓan)," and when he became angry a spark flew from him onto the earth and a spark into the sky, when they describe him as extreme in it.

I say: perhaps the reason for this metaphor is that anger is a state that occurs when the blood of the heart boils, and blood when it boils becomes greater in volume and quantity, so those vessels expand as the quantities of fluids in the body increase. Thus, the stronger the anger, the stronger the boiling, so the increase is greater, and the expansion, splitting and separation of the vessels is greater. So the mention of this concomitant was made a metonymy for the intensity of anger. If it is said: fire is not among living things, so how can it be described as enraged?

We say: the answer comes in several ways:

First: that structure is not, in our view, a condition for life, so perhaps God creates life in it while it is fire.

Second: that it likened the sound of its flame and the speed of its rushing forth to the sound and movement of an angry man.

Third: it is possible that what is meant is the rage of the guardians (al-Zabaniyah).

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 67, verses 8–10:**

The fourth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Every time a host is cast into it, its keepers will ask them, "Did no warner come to you?"﴾.

Al-fawj (a group) is a company of people, and al-afwaj (groups) are companies in succession. From this is His saying: ﴿So you will come in multitudes﴾ (al-Naba, 78:18). Khazanatuha (its keepers) are Malik and his assistants from among the zabaniyah (the angels of punishment). ﴿Did no warner come to you?﴾ is a question of reproach. Al-Zajjaj said: this reproach is an addition to their punishment. There are two issues in the verse:

Page 57

The first issue: The Murji'ah (a sect that deferred judgment on the grave sinner) argued from this verse that none enters the Fire except the disbelievers. They said: Because He, exalted is He, related of everyone who is cast into the Fire that they said, "We denied the warner." This implies that whoever does not deny Allah and His Messenger will not enter the Fire. Know that the apparent meaning of this verse requires the certainty that the persistent sinner (al-fasiq al-musirr) does not enter the Fire. The Qadi answered this by saying that the "warner" may be applied to the evidences in the intellects that warn and frighten, and no one enters the Fire except that he opposes the proof and does not hold to its requirement.

The second issue: Those who hold that knowledge of Allah and gratitude to Him are obligatory only after the revelation of scripture (al-sam') have argued with this verse. They said: This verse indicates that He punished them only because the warner came to them, and this indicates that had the warner not come to them, He would not have punished them.

Then He, exalted is He, related the disbelievers' answer to that question in two ways:

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Yes, indeed a warner came to us, but we denied and said, 'Allah has not sent down anything.'"﴾

Know that His saying ﴿Yes, indeed a warner came to us, but we denied﴾ is an acknowledgment from them of the justice of Allah, and an affirmation that Allah removed their excuses by sending the messengers. But they denied the messengers and said, ﴿Allah has not sent down anything﴾.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You are only in great error﴾, there are two issues concerning it:

The first issue: In the verse there are two views:

The first view, which is the most apparent, is that it is part of the speech of the disbelievers and their address to the warners.

The second view: It is possible that it is part of the speech of the keepers to the disbelievers, and the meaning is that when the disbelievers said that statement, the keepers said to them, ﴿You are only in great error﴾.

The second issue: It is possible that the intended "great error" is the error they were upon in the world, and it is possible that the intended "error" is destruction, and it is possible that the punishment for error was named by its name.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they said, "Had we been listening or reasoning, we would not have been among the companions of the Blaze."﴾

This is the second statement that Allah, exalted is He, related from the disbelievers as an answer to the keepers when they said, ﴿Did no warner come to you?﴾. The meaning is: Had we listened to the warning as one who was seeking the truth, or reasoned about it as one who was reflecting and pondering, we would not have been among the companions of the Blaze. It was said: He only combined hearing and reason because the basis of obligation (al-taklif) rests upon the proofs of hearing (revelation) and reason. In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: Our companions (the Ash'arites) argued with this verse on the matter of guidance and misguidance, saying: The word "law" (lau) indicates the impossibility of one thing because of the impossibility of another. The verse thus indicates that they had no hearing and no reason. But there is no doubt that they were possessors of hearing and sound intellects, and that they were not deaf nor insane. Therefore it must be that what is meant is that they had no hearing of guidance and no reason of guidance.

The second issue: Whoever said, "Religion is not complete except through instruction," argued with this verse. He said: Allah placed hearing before reason, to alert that there must first be the guidance of the guide and the direction of the one who directs, and then there follows the understanding of the one who responds and his reflection on what the teacher presents. The answer: He placed hearing first because the one invited, when he meets the Messenger, the first stage is that he hears his speech, then he reflects upon it. Since hearing precedes understanding and comprehension for this reason, it is therefore mentioned first.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 67, verse 15:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is He who made the earth subservient to you, so walk in its broad paths and eat of His provision; and to Him is the resurrection.﴾

There are several issues here.

**The first issue:** Know that the connection of this verse to what precedes it is that Allah the Exalted demonstrated by proofs that He knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Then after this He mentioned this verse as a warning. A parallel to this is one who says to his servant, who has wronged his master in secret: "O so-and-so, I know your secret and your public conduct. Sit in this house which I have given to you, all this good which I have prepared for you, and do not feel safe from my discipline. For if I wish, I can make this house, which is the abode of your security and the center of your safety, a source of the calamities in which you will be bewildered and a spring of the trials by which you will perish." Likewise here, as if Allah the Exalted said: "O disbelievers, know that I know your secret and your open speech, so be fearful of Me and beware of My punishment. This earth on whose broad paths you walk, and which you believe to be the furthest thing from harming you, is the one I made subservient to you and made a means of your benefit. So walk in its broad paths, for if I wish, I can cause this earth to swallow you up, and send down upon it from the sky all kinds of trials." This is the aspect of the connection of this verse with what precedes it.

**The second issue:** *al-dhalūl* (subservient, tractable) of anything is that which submits to you and yields. Its verbal noun is *al-dhull*, which means submission and gentleness. From it one says: "a *dābba dhalūl*" (a tame, docile riding animal). Regarding the description of the earth as *dhalūl*, there are several opinions:

First: He, the Exalted, did not make it rocky and rough such that walking on it is impossible, as walking on the rough surface of a rock is impossible.

Second: He, the Exalted, made it soft such that it is possible to dig in it and build structures from it as one wishes. Had it been hard and rocky, that would have been impossible.

Third: Had it been stony, or like gold or iron, it would have become extremely hot in summer and extremely cold in winter, cultivation in it would have been impossible, planting in it would have been unattainable, and it would not have been a place of gathering (*kifāt*) for the dead and the living.

Fourth: He, the Exalted, made it subservient to us by holding it in the atmosphere of the air. Had it been moving in a straight line or in a circular motion, it would not have been submissive to us.

**The third issue:** His words ﴿so walk in its broad paths﴾ are a command of permission (*amr ibāḥa*, a command indicating permissibility), and the same applies to His words ﴿and eat of His provision﴾.

**The fourth issue:** The commentators have mentioned several meanings for "the broad paths of the earth" (*manākib al-arḍ*):

First: The author of *al-Kashshāf* said: Walking in its broad paths is a metaphor (*mathal*) for the extreme of making it subservient. This is because the two shoulders of a camel and the place where they meet at the back (*al-gharib*) are the thinnest part of the camel and the least possible part on which to walk. So when the camel becomes such that it is possible to walk upon its shoulder, it has reached the extreme of submission and obedience. Thus it is established that His words ﴿so walk in its broad paths﴾ are an allusion (*kināya*) to the earth being at the extreme of tractability.

Second: The saying of Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Abbas: The broad paths of the earth are its mountains and hills. The mountains were called *manākib* (shoulders) because the shoulders of a human are prominent, and the mountains are also prominent. The meaning is: I have made it easy for you to walk in its broad paths, which are the parts farthest from being tractable, so how much more so in its other parts.

Third: The broad paths are the roads, the wide passes, the edges and the sides. This is the saying of al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Kalbi and Muqatil, a narration from Ata from Ibn Abbas, the preference of al-Farra', and Ibn Qutayba, who said: "Its *manākib* are its sides, and the two *manकib* of a man are his two sides." This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah has made the earth a spread-out carpet for you﴾ ﴿so that you may traverse therein its wide roads﴾ (Nuh 19–20).

As for His words ﴿and eat of His provision﴾, meaning of what Allah has created as provision for you in the earth. ﴿And to Him is the resurrection﴾ means: your sojourn on the earth and your eating of the provision of Allah should be the sojourn of one who knows that his return is to Allah, and the eating of one who is certain that his destination is Allah. The purpose is to warn them against disbelief and sins, whether in secret or in public. Then Allah the Exalted explained that their continued survival with this safety on the earth was only by the grace and mercy of Allah, and that if He willed, He would turn the matter against them and rain down upon them from the cloud of His subjugation a rain of calamities.

أمّا الثّانِي فَهو قَوْلُهُ: ﴿أمَّنْ هَذا الَّذِي يَرْزُقُكم إنْ أمْسَكَ رِزْقَهُ﴾ .

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿أمَّنْ هَذا الَّذِي هو جُنْدٌ لَكم يَنْصُرُكم مِن دُونِ الرَّحْمَنِ إنِ الكافِرُونَ إلّا في غُرُورٍ﴾ .

أحَدُهُما: القُوَّةُ الَّتِي كانَتْ حاصِلَةً لَهم بِسَبَبِ مالِهِمْ وجُنْدِهِمْ.

The second proof of His complete power is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: It is He who brought you into being and made for you hearing, sight and hearts. Little is it that you give thanks.﴾

Know that when He, exalted, presented the first proof (burhan) from the condition of the other animals, namely the standing of birds in the air, He presented after it a proof from the condition of human beings, which is this verse. He mentioned among its wonders the condition of hearing, sight and the heart (fu'ad). The explanation of the states of these three faculties has already been given many times in this book, so there is no benefit in repeating it. Know that mentioning them here contains an alert to a subtle point, as if He, exalted, said: I gave you these three bestowals together with the noble faculties within them, but you wasted them. You did not accept what you heard, you did not take heed from what you saw, and you did not reflect upon the outcome of what you understood. So it is as if you have squandered these blessings and corrupted these gifts. Therefore He said: ﴿little is it that you give thanks﴾. This is because giving thanks for the blessing of God, exalted is to direct that blessing toward what pleases Him. Since you have directed hearing, sight and intellect not toward seeking His good pleasure, you have not given thanks for His blessing at all.

The third proof: His saying, ﴿Say, "It is He who produced you on the earth, and to Him you will be gathered."﴾

Know that He, exalted, first argued from the conditions of animals, then second from the attributes of man, namely hearing, sight and reason, and third from the origination of his essence, which is His saying: ﴿It is He who produced you on the earth﴾. The mutakallimun (scholars of kalam, Islamic dialectical theology) used this verse to argue that man is not the simple substance (al-jawhar al-mujarrad) free of spatial occupation (tahayyuz) and quantity (kammiyyah), as the philosophers (falasifah) and a group of Muslims maintain. The first of them: they asked him to specify the time, which is His saying, exalted: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾.

On this there are issues:

The first issue: Abu Muslim said: He, exalted, said "yaqulu" (they say) in the present/future form, so this may refer to what the disbelievers say of this statement in the future, and it may refer to the past, the implied meaning being: "they used to say this promise."

The second issue: Perhaps they were saying that in mockery, and perhaps they were saying it to mislead the weak-minded, that since it had not come quickly, it has no basis.

The third issue: What is the promise being asked about? On this there are two views:

One of them: it is the Resurrection (al-qiyamah).

The second: it is punishment in general (mutlaq al-'adhab).

The benefit of this difference will become apparent afterwards, God willing.

Then He, exalted is He, described their state when that promise came to pass, saying: ﴿But when they see it approaching, the faces of those who disbelieved will be darkened﴾. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿when they see it﴾ — the pronoun refers to the promise. Zulfah (zulfah) means nearness, so the sense is: "when they see it near." It is said: sa'a al-shay'u yasu'u, fa-huwa sayyi' if it became ugly, and si'a yusa'u if it became ugly; it is both intransitive and transitive. So the meaning of "their faces were made ugly" is that they became disfigured, with gloom covering them, eclipse (kusuf) and dust overtaking them, and they grimaced, and their faces became like the face of one who is being led to execution.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it will be said, "This is what you used to call for."﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Some said: the ones who say it are the Zabaniyah (guardian angels of Hell). Others said: rather, some of them say it to others.

The second issue: Regarding His saying ﴿tadda'un﴾ there are several aspects:

First: al-Farra' said: he means tadda'un from du'a', i.e., you seek it and hasten for it; and tad'un and tadda'un are the same in the language, like tadhkurun and tadhdhakkarun, and tadkharun and taddakharun.

Second: that it is from da'wa (claim), meaning: "This is what you used to deny," i.e., you claimed that it is false and would not come to you; or "This is what because of which you used to claim that you would not be resurrected."

Third: that this is an interrogative in the sense of denunciation, and the meaning is: "Is this what you used to claim? No, rather you used to claim its non-existence."

The third issue: Ya'qub al-Hadrami recited (tad'un) with a light (khafifah) form from du'a', and the Seven (readers) recited (tadda'un) with a heavy (muthaqqalah) form from ida'a'.

**The Word of Allah, the Exalted:** ﴿Say: "Have you considered: if Allah destroys me and those with me, or has mercy on us, who will protect the disbelievers from a painful punishment?"﴾

Know that this reply is of the second type of what the disbelievers said to Muhammad (ﷺ) when he warned them of the punishment of Allah. It is related that the disbelievers of Makkah used to call down destruction upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and upon the believers, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Or do they say, "A poet, for whom we await the misfortunes of time"?﴾ (al-Tur: 30), and He said: ﴿Rather, you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families again﴾ (al-Fath: 12). Then Allah answered them in two ways.

The first way is this verse. The meaning is: say to them, "Whether Allah destroys me by causing me to die, or has mercy on me by delaying my appointed term, it is the same. What comfort is there for you in that, and what benefit is there for you in it? And who will protect you from the punishment of Allah when it descends upon you? Do you think the idols will protect you, or something else? So if you know that there is no protector for you, then why do you not hold fast to what will save you from the punishment, which is knowledge of the Oneness (tawhid) of Allah, prophethood (nubuwwah), and resurrection (ba'th)?"

The second way is in the answer given by His saying: ﴿Say: "He is the Most Merciful. We have believed in Him, and upon Him we have relied. So you will know who is in clear error."﴾

The meaning is: He is the Most Merciful. "We have believed in Him and upon Him we have relied," so He knows that He does not accept your supplication against us, while you are the people of disbelief and obstinacy towards us, although we have believed in Him and have not disbelieved in Him as you have disbelieved. Then He said: ﴿and upon Him we have relied﴾, not upon anyone else, as you did, when you relied upon your men and your wealth. The verb (فَسَتَعْلَمُونَ, fa-sata'lamuna, "you will know") was read in the second person (addressing them), and it was also read with the ya' (يَعْلَمُونَ, ya'lamuna, "they will know"), so that it would conform to His saying: ﴿who will protect the disbelievers﴾.

Know that when He mentioned that one must rely upon Him alone and not upon anyone else, and mentioned the evidence for that, He said: ﴿Say: "Have you considered: if your water should sink into the earth, who then will bring you flowing water?"﴾

The purpose is to make them acknowledge some of His blessings, so that He may show them the ugliness of the disbelief they are upon. That is: tell me, if your water becomes lost in the earth, who will bring you flowing water? They must say, "It is Allah." Then it will be said to them: "Why then do you make one who has no power over anything at all a partner with Him in worship?" This is like His saying: ﴿Have you considered the water that you drink?﴾ ﴿Is it you who brought it down from the cloud, or are We the Sender?﴾ (al-Waqi'ah: 68–69).

As for His saying: ﴿ghawran﴾ (غَوْرًا), it means "sunk, going away into the earth." It is said: "the water sank (ghara al-ma' yaghuru ghawran)" when it recedes and goes away into the earth. Here, ghawr (غَوْر) is in the sense of "sinking," but it was expressed by the verbal noun, as one says "a just man" (rajul 'adl) and "a content man" (rajul ridan). Al-ma'in (المَعِين) is the apparent water that the eyes see; it is from the passive sense of "the eye," like mabi' (مَبِيع, "sold"). It was also said that al-ma'in is that which flows from springs, from the intensity of flowing (al-imān fi al-jary), as if it were said: "one who flows intensely."

And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best. May Allah send blessings upon our master Muhammad, and upon his family and companions, and grant them peace.
